exhibits.name: LexGuard
exhibits.pitch: Contract review under Indian law, where written rules can overrule the model.
exhibits.problem: A contract reviewer that is right most of the time is easy to demo and hard to trust. LLMs under-rate predatory clauses written in calm legal language: the trap reads as boilerplate, so it comes back LOW.
exhibits.approach: A staged agent pipeline extracts clauses, rates risk, checks Indian statutes and drafts rewrites. Before any of those agents reads a risk level, a deterministic auditor runs hand-written trap patterns and can force an escalation. Every statute the model cites is looked up and graded before the user sees it.
hard: Fitting in 512 MB of RAM: a 380 MB V8 heap cap, local embedding models unloaded when idle, and a forced GC after every job.
Providers fail mid-document, so the AI client falls through Gemini, Groq, Hugging Face, Grok and local Ollama instead of failing the job.
PDFs glue section numbers onto the previous sentence. A two-pass chunker repairs the text before any model sees it.
Clause IDs echoed back by the LLM drifted onto the wrong clause, so clauses are keyed by their position in the document instead.
exhibits.limits: The committed benchmark reports were run before I removed rules copied from the benchmark, so they may overstate current accuracy; a re-run is pending. I also wrote both the test clauses and the trap patterns, so the suites catch regressions, not generalisation.

claims.text: Deterministic rules run before any LLM agent reads a risk level, so the model cannot talk a clause down.
Every statute the model cites is looked up and graded before it is shown.
Rules copied from the benchmark's own text were deleted, even though they raised the score.

exhibits.name: Pikina
exhibits.pitch: An offline-first desktop assistant that asks before it acts and can undo what it did.
exhibits.problem: An assistant that can touch your files and apps is only useful if you can see, and stop, what it is about to do. Most assistants send your screen to a server and act first.
exhibits.approach: Known intents go through regex-first routing; everything else goes to a local model through Ollama. Every action the model proposes is checked against a capability registry, passes one shared consent rule, and multi-step plans run as transactions that roll back when a step fails.
hard: Keeping one consent rule true across three entry points (hotkey, local model and API), so no path can skip the gate.
Making rollback real: an action is only allowed to run unattended at level 3 if it declares how to undo itself.
exhibits.limits: Pre-alpha. The task scheduler is built and tested, but nothing calls it until the planner lands.

claims.text: Nothing the model proposes reaches a tool without a schema check against the capability registry.
One consent rule for every path: level 4 always asks; level 3 asks when the action can't be rolled back.

claims.text: Multi-step plans roll back step by step when one fails.

exhibits.name: Noesis
exhibits.pitch: Search across video, audio, PDFs and images, with answers pinned to a timestamp or page.
exhibits.problem: Text-only RAG misses what is said in a lecture video or drawn on a slide, and an answer with no timestamp or page number can't be checked.
exhibits.approach: Video, audio, PDFs and images are turned into one chunk schema with a time window or page attached. Retrieval fuses dense and BM25 results, a local cross-encoder reranks them, and a separate fact-audit pass labels every claim in the answer supported, partially supported or unsupported.
hard: Exact terms (names, formulas, error codes) get lost by embeddings, and paraphrases get lost by BM25, so it needs both, fused.
A grounded answer is only checkable if each chunk remembers where it came from, so location is part of the schema, not an afterthought.
exhibits.limits: Built with Apurva Patil as a Streamlit prototype; it has not been run on a large corpus.

claims.text: Dense and BM25 results are merged with reciprocal rank fusion.
Reranking runs on a local cross-encoder, not a paid API.
A second pass audits every claim in the answer as supported, partially supported or unsupported.
Every source is cited by its time window in a recording or its page in a document.

exhibits.name: Resilion
exhibits.pitch: Turns news into structured supply-chain risk and traces who gets hit.
exhibits.problem: Supply-chain risk shows up as news prose. Deciding which industries a port closure or a strike actually affects needs structure, not a summary.
exhibits.approach: Gemini extracts structured risk events from articles; validators reject any event type, severity or trade corridor the graph doesn't know. Graph traversal then finds the industries downstream of the disruption and scores how exposed each one is.
hard: Stopping the model from inventing places: an extracted corridor must already exist in the seeded graph, or the field stays empty.
exhibits.limits: The supply graph and the Risk Watcher work. Rerouting, the API and the approval console are planned, not built.

claims.text: The model can't invent a trade corridor: extracted events must name a seeded one, or none.
A disruption is traced through the supply graph to the industries it affects.

exhibits.name: HostelDesk
exhibits.pitch: Hostel complaints with honest ETAs, automatic routing and escalation.
exhibits.problem: Hostel complaints vanish into a queue with no date and no reason. Students chase staff; staff can't see their own backlog.
exhibits.approach: Tickets are routed to the right staff member automatically. Each staff queue is simulated to produce an ETA range, a delay comes with a plain-language reason, and a background job escalates anything past its deadline.
hard: An ETA is only honest if it accounts for everything already in that person's queue, so ETAs come from simulating the whole queue, not a fixed SLA.
exhibits.limits: Deployed on Neon and Render. The ML features on its roadmap are planned, not built.

exhibits.name: C++ Shell
exhibits.pitch: A POSIX-style shell: quoting, redirection, pipelines and background jobs.
exhibits.problem: The shell is the tool everyone uses and few people have built. I wanted to know what actually happens between pressing Enter and seeing output.
exhibits.approach: Builtins, PATH lookup, a quoting state machine, I/O redirection, multi-stage pipelines and background jobs, built directly on fork, exec, pipe and dup2.
hard: File descriptors: every pipe end a child doesn't use has to be closed, or the next stage waits forever for an EOF that never comes.
exhibits.limits: Built along the CodeCrafters shell track, so the feature list follows its stages.

claims.text: Pipelines are wired by hand with pipe() and fork(), not a library.
Each stage's stdin is the previous stage's pipe, rewired with dup2().
Quoting is parsed by its own state machine for single and double quotes.

exhibits.name: ShopKart
exhibits.pitch: A store whose checkout never trusts the browser with a price.
exhibits.problem: A checkout that trusts the price the browser sends can be edited into a discount, and a payment the client says succeeded may not have.
exhibits.approach: The server rebuilds every order from database prices and live stock, and an order is only marked paid after Razorpay's signature checks out with HMAC-SHA256 on the server.
exhibits.limits: Razorpay runs in test mode. Built with Apurva Patil.

claims.text: Order totals are recomputed on the server from database prices; the client's total is ignored.
A payment counts only after its Razorpay signature is verified with HMAC-SHA256.

exhibits.name: Meta OpenEnv
exhibits.pitch: An agent environment where finishing the work by burning out still loses points.
exhibits.problem: Agent benchmarks reward getting things done. Few of them penalise an agent for scheduling a person into the ground to do it.
exhibits.approach: An OpenEnv environment where an agent plans assignments, bugs and features against hard deadlines. The graders reward finished work and add bonuses only for burnout-free (no day over 8 hours) and balanced schedules.
exhibits.limits: A team submission to the Meta PyTorch OpenEnv Hackathon.

principles.title: Rules decide what must never be wrong. Models handle the rest.
principles.body: A language model is a good first reader and a bad final judge. When a mistake is expensive, a plain rule gets the last word.

principles.title: Ask before anything you can't undo.
principles.body: Consent is cheap when it is rare. If an action can be rolled back, let it run; if it can't, stop and ask.

principles.title: Every answer points to its source.
principles.body: A citation that can't be opened is decoration. Statutes are looked up, and answers point to a page or a timestamp.

principles.title: Don't grade yourself on the test you wrote.
principles.body: A rule that matches the benchmark measures memory, not judgement. I deleted those rules and the score came with them.

principles.title: Never trust the client with money.
principles.body: Prices come from the database and payments from a verified signature. The browser only gets to ask.

principles.title: Tell people why, not just when.
principles.body: A date with no reason creates follow-up messages. A reason makes waiting easier.

principles.title: Build the boring layer by hand at least once.
principles.body: You understand a pipe after you have leaked one.
